# Spaceflight alters protein levels and gene expression associated with stress response and metabolic characteristics in human cardiac spheroids

**Authors:** Parvin Forghani; Wenhao Liu; Zeyu Wang; Zhi Ling; Felipe Takaesu; Evan Yang; Gregory K. Tharp; Sheila Nielsen; Shankini Doraisingam; Stefanie Countryman; Michael E. Davis; Ronghu Wu; Shu Jia; Chunhui Xu

**Affiliations:** 1Department of Pediatrics, Emory University School of Medicine and Children’s Healthcare of Atlanta, Atlanta, GA, USA | 2Wallace H. Coulter Department of Biomedical Engineering, Georgia Institute of Technology and Emory University, Atlanta, GA, USA | 3School of Chemistry and Biochemistry, Georgia Institute of Technology, Atlanta, GA, USA | 4Emory National Primate Research Center, Emory University; Atlanta, Georgia, USA | 5BioServe Space Technologies, Boulder, CO, USA

## Abstract

Cardiomyocytes derived from human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSC-CMs) possess tremendous advantage for cardiac regeneration. However, cell survival is challenging upon cell transplantation. Since microgravity can profoundly affect cellular properties, we investigated the effect of spaceflight on hiPSC-CMs. Cardiac spheroids derived from hiPSCs were transported to the International Space Station (ISS) via the SpaceX Crew-8 mission and cultured under space microgravity for 8 days. Beating cardiac spheroids were observed on the ISS and upon successful experimentation by the astronauts in space, the live cultures were returned to Earth. These cells had normal displacement (an indicator of contraction) and Ca2+ transient parameters in 3D live cell imaging. Proteomic analysis revealed that spaceflight upregulated many proteins involved in metabolism (n=90), cellular component of mitochondrion (n=62) and regulation of proliferation (n=10). Specific metabolic pathways enriched by spaceflight included glutathione metabolism, biosynthesis of amino acids, and pyruvate metabolism. In addition, the top upregulated proteins in spaceflight samples included those involved in cellular stress response, cell survival, and metabolism. Transcriptomic profiles indicated that spaceflight upregulated genes associated with cardiomyocyte development, and cellular components of cardiac structure and mitochondrion. Furthermore, spaceflight upregulated genes in metabolic pathways associated with cell survival such as glycerophospholipid metabolism and glycerolipid metabolism. These findings indicate that short-term exposure of 3D hiPSC-CMs to the space environment led to significant changes in protein levels and gene expression involved in cell survival and metabolism.

## Introduction

Heart disease is the leading cause of death in the United States, and cell replacement therapy is a promising approach to improve heart function [1]. Among potential cell candidates, cardiomyocytes derived from human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSC-CMs) could provide an inexhaustible source of cells to treat heart disease, owing to the ability of hiPSCs to self-renew extensively at undifferentiated state and to differentiate into functional cardiomyocytes [2–5]. In preclinical studies, human stem cell-derived cardiomyocytes or cardiac progenitors prevented progression of heart failure [6–12] and functioned as a biological pacemaker [13–15]. For example, following transplantation, human stem cell-derived cardiomyocytes survived in infarcted rat hearts and contributed to cardiac function [6, 16]. Preclinical studies using large animals also demonstrated feasibility and therapeutic efficacy of human stem cell-derived cardiomyocytes [17–20]. Furthermore, several clinical trials have been initiated, including a trial using purified human stem cell-derived cardiac progenitors to treat patients with heart failure [21]. Case reports of a clinical trial also indicated that transplantation of hiPSC-CM patch was feasible, although accumulation of data from additional patients is needed to confirm safety and efficacy for treatment of ischemic cardiomyopathy [22]. These preclinical and clinical research and development portend a promising future for cardiac cell therapy with stem cell-derived cardiomyocytes, but many issues warrant further investigation for clinical translation.

Among many critical issues, new strategies are needed to improve survival of transplanted cardiomyocytes in host tissue for cardiac regeneration [23]. Poor cell survival after transplantation has been reported in multiple independent studies [24–26]. Significant bioengineering efforts are underway to overcome the limitation of poor cell survival, including co-transplantation of microvessels to improve cardiomyocyte engraftment [23]. Poor cell survival is likely due to multiple factors of the stress environment including the hypoxic conditions of the injured heart. These preclinical studies underscore the importance of identifying molecular factors/pathways that allow hiPSC-CMs to overcome stress conditions and improve their ability to survive. As a billon cardiomyocytes are needed for each patient in transplantation, to compensate for the large loss of cells in a typical injured heart [3], hiPSC-CMs with enhanced survival potential are critical for successful cardiac cell therapy. Ways for allowing cells to overcome stress environments not only enhance graft survival but also help reduce the burden of cell production.

Microgravity is known to be able to significantly affect cell characteristics with various outcomes depending on cell types and culture durations. In particular, the International Space Station (ISS) has provided a unique environment for discovery of novel biological processes and molecular signaling/pathways in response to microgravity. For examples, human cardiovascular progenitors had improved growth and migration following a >30 days culture on the ISS [27]. Human mesenchymal stem cells had increased immunosuppressive capacity following a 2-week culture on the ISS, a desirable feature for the use of these cells in therapy [28]. hiPSC-derived cardiac progenitors had improved cell proliferation and differentiation following exposure to space microgravity for 3 weeks [29, 30]. And monolayer late-stage hiPSC-CMs cultured on the ISS for >30 days had increased expression of genes associated with mitochondrial metabolism [31].

In this study, we investigated molecular alterations of hiPSC-CMs in response to spaceflight by growing these cells in spheroids on the ISS. The spheroids were cryopreserved on the ground and cultured under space microgravity for 8 days. Control cells were cultured on the ground using the same cell culture device. On the ISS, astronauts successfully cultured the cells and sent back beating cardiomyocytes. Following sample return, we examined function of the cells by live cell 3D imaging and investigated molecular alterations of these cells by omics analyses.

## Materials and methods

### Cell culture and cardiomyocyte differentiation

hiPSCs [iPS(IMR90)-4, WiCell Research Institute] were maintained in mTeSR (STEMCELL Technologies) and induced for cardiac differentiation using growth factors [6, 32]. Briefly, cells were treated with 100 ng/mL recombinant human activin A (R&D Systems) in RPMI medium with 2% B27 insulin-free (RPMI/B27 insulin-free medium) on days 0. After 24 h, the medium was replaced with 10 ng/mL recombinant human bone morphogenic protein-4 (BMP4; R&D Systems) in RPMI/B27 insulin-free medium from day 1 to day 4. The medium was changed to RPMI medium with 2% B27 containing insulin (RPMI/B27 medium) on differentiation day 5.

### Formation of cardiac spheroids

Cardiac spheroids were generated on differentiation day 9 as follows. Cells were dissociated with 0.25% trypsin-EDTA and seeded into AggreWell 400 plates (Stem Cell Technologies) at 1,500 cells/microwell to allow cells to form cardiac spheroids. Before cell seeding, plates with 1 mL/well of RPMI/B27 medium were centrifuged at 1,000 g to release trapped bubbles in microwells. To prevent cell death, medium was supplemented with 10 μM ROCK inhibitor Y-27632 (Selleck Chemicals). After cell seeding, plates were centrifuged at 100 g to distribute the cells and then placed in an incubator. After 24 h, spheroids were harvested to remove ROCK inhibitor and were replaced in the suspension culture in RPMI/B27 medium.

### Cryopreservation of cardiac spheroids and thawing procedure

The 2X cryopreservation medium containing 80% Knockout Serum Replacement (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and 20% dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) was freshly prepared on the day of cryopreservation. Cells were harvested from AggreWell plates and transferred into 50-mL centrifuge tubes. The AggreWell plates were examined under a microscope to make sure that most of the cardiac spheroids were harvested. Cardiac spheroids were allowed to be settled down upon centrifugation. Cells from one AggreWell plate were used to load into one vial. Cells were resuspended by gently tapping the tube, and then adding Knockout Serum Replacement (500 μL/vial) and subsequently cold 2X cryopreservation medium (500 μL/vial). Cells were incubated for 30 min, then transferred into a freezing container, and stored at −80°C. After at least 24 h, cells were transferred to the liquid nitrogen tank for long-term storage.

To thaw cells, cryopreserved cells were transferred to 37°C. After 4 min, 500 μL to 1 mL thawing medium was added to the vial and the thawed cells were then inoculated into a tube and centrifuged at 1,000 rpm for 3 min to remove DMSO. The thawing medium contained Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle Medium (DMEM, Thermo Fisher Scientific) supplemented with 15% Knockout Serum Replacement, 1% GlutaMAX-I (Thermo Fisher Scientific), and 1% Antibiotic Antimycotic Solution (Sigma-Aldrich). Cells were transferred to suspension cultures in the thawing medium and monitored immediately and 1–2 days post thawing. Two days post thawing, ~90% of the medium was exchanged using the maturation medium composed of DMEM supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (Corning), 1% GlutaMAX, 1% Antibiotic Antimycotic Solution and 4 g/L AlbuMAX II Lipid-rich BSA (Thermo Fisher Scientific).

### Hardware design

To meet the requirement of suspension cultures, BioServe team designed a new version of the BioCell cell culture module (dual chamber 1-well BioCell), which has a filtering membrane in the middle to separate the cell and medium chambers. The cell chamber is used to load the cells and the medium chamber is used for medium exchange. The filtering membrane has a pore size of 4.0 μm that allows nutrients but not cells to pass through between the two chambers.

After loading the cells, the Biocells were placed in custom-designed flight hardware (Plate Habitat; PHAB) which had the capacity for three Biocells. The PHABs were used to transport live cells to the launch site, to the ISS and return to Earth. The PHABs were charged with 5% CO2 with vents opened and then sealed with a Kempton tape cover to maintain 4.5–5% CO2. The sealed PHABs were placed in a container that maintained temperature at ~37°C for transportation.

### Characterization of differentiation cultures

To confirm differentiation quality before making spheroids and cryopreservation, we first performed QC Level I. Randomly selected wells of differentiation cultures on day 6 post differentiation were dissociated with 0.25% trypsin-EDTA and reseeded in Matrigel-coated 96-well culture plates at a density of 2.5–3 ×105 cells/well in RPMI/B27 medium containing 10 μM ROCK inhibitor. For post-thawing testing (QC Level II), similar procedures of cell seeding were performed using cells 8 days post-thawing.

One day after cell seeding, the cells were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde for 15 min following a gentle PBS wash. The cells were then permeabilized using 90% cold methanol for 2 min at room temperature (RT). The cells were blocked with 5% normal goat serum (NGS) in PBS at RT for 1 h and incubated at RT with the optimized concentrations of primary antibodies against NKX2.5 (Cell Signaling; 1:1,200) and α-actinin (Sigma-Aldrich; 1:800) diluted in 3% NGS for the purity assay.

After the incubation with the primary antibodies, the cells were washed twice with PBS and incubated with secondary antibodies: Alexa Fluor 488 conjugated goat anti-mouse IgG1 (for α-actinin staining; Life Technologies) and Alexa Fluor 594 conjugated goat anti-rabbit IgG (for NKX2–5 staining; Life Technologies) diluted at 1:1,000 in PBS with 1.5% NGS. The nuclei were counterstained with Hoechst 33342 (Thermo Fisher Scientific) for 15 min at RT and pre-imaged using an inverted microscope (Axio Vert.A1). Stained cells were quantitatively analyzed using Cytation 5 (Agilent). Data analysis was performed using Gene 5 3.13 Software for Cytation 5. Sixteen fields/well were imaged and the average percentage of NKX2.5 and α-actinin-positive cells was used as the final readout.

### Preparation of ISS and ground BioCells and pre-launch procedures

Biocells were filled with the maturation medium (60 ml/Biocell) made freshly on the day of cell inoculation. Cells were thawed a few days ahead of time and maintained in the thawing medium before they were inoculated into BioCells through cell chamber using an 18-gauge needle. One day after cell inoculation, we examined the BioCells and removed any bubbles if needed. Insulated boxes with heater adapters for temperature maintenance control during transportation were prepared by BioServe group to transport live cells in Biocells during travel.

At the launch site, 6 × 30 mL syringes were filled with freshly made maturation medium for two possible medium exchange procedures. The needles were then replaced with recapped tools to seal the syringes. A few hours later syringes were examined, and extra bubbles were removed if presented. The syringes were then stored at −80°C to be ready for handover. Medium without antibiotic added was inoculated into the LB medium to test sterility.

### Live cell imaging of Ca2+ transients and displacement using Fourier light-field microscopy (FLFM)

On the day of imaging, the staining solution of Calbryte 520 AM (AAT Bioquest) at a final concentration of 10 μM was made by first adding 4.56 μL DMSO (Thermo Fisher Scientific) into one vial of Calbryte 520 AM, and then diluting it at a ratio 1:1000 into prewarmed OptiMEM medium (Thermo Fisher Scientific) with supplements of 1% glucose (Thermo Fisher Scientific), 1% non-essential amino acid (NEAA, Thermo Fisher Scientific) and 2 g/L AlbuMAX II (Thermo Fisher Scientific). For staining, the culture medium was replaced with the staining solution, and the cells were incubated for 50 min at 37°C. The staining medium was then removed, and the cells were washed twice with 3 mL prewarmed PBS (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Subsequently, the cells were incubated for 20 min at 37°C in 3 mL hiPSC-CM medium for recovery. After the incubation, the cells were washed twice with 3 mL prewarmed PBS again and then placed in FluoroBrite DMEM (Thermo Fisher Scientific) with supplements of 1% GlutaMAX, 1% NEAA and 2 g/L AlbuMAX II for imaging.

Cardiac spheroids loaded with Calbryte 520 AM were imaged using a homemade FLFM system [33], and movies of 15 sec were taken at 125 Hz for each cardiac spheroid sample. The FLFM was equipped with a water-dipping physiology objective lens (CFI75 LWD 16×/0.8 W, Nikon) and used a 300-mm tube lens (AC508–300-A-ML, Thorlabs), a 200-mm Fourier lens (AC508–200-A-ML, Thorlabs), and a customized microlens array MLA that consists 3 by 3 planoconvex lenses which are 3.3 mm square with 30-mm focal length as described [34]. The sample was illuminated with a light-emitting diode (LED) peaked at 470 nm (M470L5, Thorlabs), and a filter set (MF469-35, ZET488/594rpc, ZET488/594m, Chroma) was adopted.

Videos were recorded on an sCMOS camera (ORCA-Flash-4.0 v3, Hamamatsu) at a frame rate of 125 Hz with the control software HCImage, which is developed by Hamamatsu, and were written into a PCIe 3.0 NVMe solid-state drive (SSD, SAMSUNG 970 EVO Plus) as files in ‘.dcimg’ format. Moreover, for experiments in the same illumination conditions, a video without sample but in the same experimental and illumination conditions was taken to record the background offset. In the first step of data processing, each video taken was converted by HCImage to TIFF images of 16 bits in an individual folder, and the frames of background offset were averaged. Then, for each frame, the image was subtracted by the average background offset, and the elemental images were cropped out. Next, each elemental image in a frame was cropped into the desired field of view, and all cropped elemental images were stitched back to form a light-field image covering only the region of interest (ROI). Further, each video was denoised using an algorithm called MIRO [35], which leverages shearlet optimal sparse representation to extract biological features from noise in the spatial domain and implements a time-based collaborative wiener filter on the temporal domain to remove the fluorescence fluctuation in the background.

Each video was normalized individually, and from the time-lapsed frames of a video, 3D volumes of the sample space were reconstructed sequentially via Richardson-Lucy deconvolution (RLD) by using a hybrid point spread function (hPSF), which was generated by calibrating the numerically simulated PSF with an experimentally recorded one [36]. The experimental PSF was obtained by imaging single-layer sparse 2-μm fluorescent beads across a depth range of ± 40 μm on the same day we imaged the CMs. Hybrid-PSF was cropped into the same size as the cropped image of 3DCMs, and its corresponding optical transfer function (OTF) was generated as an input variable to avoid repetitive calculation in the iteration. RLD was conducted via 20 iterations for the reconstruction of each frame and was accelerated using graphic cards (A6000, NVidia) to realize parallel processing.

The magnification of the system is 3.6, and thus, the pixel size in the sample space is 6.5 μm/3.6=1806 nm. The axial step size of the hPSF is 800 nm, and as a result, the voxel of the reconstructed space was 1806×1806×800 nm3. In post-processing, the reconstructed space was first interpolated to the voxel size of 800×800×800 nm3. Then, in each 3D hiPSC-CMs, the initial positions of the cells were recognized by finding the local maxima in the smoothed 3D reconstructed volume. To track the cells over time, we utilize a process that involves fitting a 7×7×11-voxel volume centered on the previous center of each cluster to a 3D Gaussian function. The resulting peak of the Gaussian function was then used as the center of the volume window in the subsequent time frame. As the 3D positions of all clusters do not overlap in this scenario, we can track the position of each cluster independently and automatically by identifying the Gaussian window to the previous time point. Since the calcium indicator was tagged to the cytosol of the hiPSC-CMs, we quantified the Ca2+ trace over the period by calculating the average intensity of all pixels within the 3×3×5 volume.

### Proteomic analysis

Cell lysis and digestion were performed as described previously [32]. Briefly, proteins were extracted by suspending the cells in the lysis buffer (50 mM HEPES pH=8, 150 mM NaCl, 0.5% SDC, 25 units/mL benzonase, and 1 tablet/10 mL protease inhibitor) at 4°C for 45 min. Protein concentration was determined by the BCA assay, and proteins in all samples were then normalized based on their measured concentrations. Proteins were reduced with 5 mM Dithiothreitol (56°C, 30 min), followed by alkylation with 14 mM iodoacetamide (RT, 30 minutes in the dark). They were purified through methanol–chloroform protein precipitation. For secretome analysis, the medium was first passed through a filter (0.45 μm) and then concentrated by centrifugation (3 kDa cutoff). The other steps were the same as described for the cell lysates.

Proteins were digested with trypsin in a buffer containing 50 mM HEPES (pH 8.5), 1.6 M urea at 37°C overnight. After the digestion, peptides were purified using tC18 Sep-Pak cartridges. For running LC-MS/MS, peptide samples were dissolved in a solvent containing 5% ACN (acetonitrile) and 4% formic acid (FA), and 4 μL was loaded using a Dionex WPS-3000TPLRS autosampler (UltiMate 3000 Thermostatted Rapid Separation Pulled Loop Well plate Sampler) onto a microcapillary column packed with C18 beads (Magic C18AQ, 1.9 μm, 200 Å, 75 μm × 16 cm, Michrom Bioresources). Peptides were separated by a reverse-phase nano HPLC (Dionex Ultimate 3000 RSLC Nano system) using a 95 min gradient of 2–24% ACN with 0.125% FA. The peptides were analyzed by an Orbitrap Exploris 480 mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific) with a data independent acquisition (DIA) method as previously reported [37, 38]. MS1 spectra were collected in the range of 420–680 at the resolution of 60,000 and AGC (Automatic Gain Control) was set as 3×106. MS2 spectra were collected at m/z 430–670 at the resolution of 30,000 with the isolation windows of 4 m/z without overlapping. The AGC target was set as 3×106 and the maximum injection time was set as “auto”. Stepped normalized collision energies of 22, 26, and 30% were used.

The raw files were searched against the Homo sapiens proteome database downloaded from UniProt (2023-03-06) using FragPipe (v21.1) with MSFragger (v4.0) [39]. Workflow “DIA_SpecLib_Quant” was loaded for spectral library building and protein quantification [40]. Briefly, the precursor and fragment mass tolerance were set as 20 ppm. The enzyme specificity was set as fully tryptic, and the maximum missed cleavage was set as 1. The peptide length was set as 7–50. The variable modifications included methionine oxidation (+15.9949 Da) and protein N-terminal acetylation (+42.0106 Da). The fixed modification was cysteine alkylation (+57.02146 Da). PSM and protein identification were filtered to a false discovery rate (FDR) of less than 1% through Philosopher module in FragPipe [41]. The proteins were quantified using DIA-NN module with the default setting. The downstream statistical analysis and visualization were conducted via FragPipe-Analyst [42]. Variance stabilizing normalization was selected and applied, while other parameters were kept at their default settings.

For proteomics, differentially expressed proteins were filtered based on thresholds abundance>1.3 fold [log2(1.3)=0.38] and P-value<0.05. Functional annotation and pathway enrichment (Gene Ontology (GO) analysis and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathway analysis were performed using two bioinformatic tools, the Database for Annotation, Visualization, and Integrated Discovery (DAVID) [43] and Metascape [44].

### RNA extraction and RNA Sequencing (RNA-seq)

RNA was isolated using Aurum total RNA mini kit (Bio-Rad) according to manufacturer’s instructions. Upon testing RNA integrity, sequencing data was acquired on an Illumina NovaSeq 6000 funded by NIH S10 OD026799. RNA quality was assessed using a TapeStation 4200 (Agilent) and then ten nanograms of total RNA was used as input for cDNA synthesis using the Clontech SMART-Seq v4 Ultra Low Input RNA kit (Takara Bio) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Amplified cDNA was fragmented and appended with dual-indexed barcodes using the Nextera XT DNA Library Preparation kit (Illumina). Libraries were validated by capillary electrophoresis on a TapeStation 4200 (Agilent), pooled at equimolar concentrations, and sequenced with PE100 reads on an Illumina NovaSeq 6000, yielding ~25 million reads per sample on average. Sequences were aligned in Galaxy using Trim-Galore and Bowtie2 and the hg38 reference genome. Samples that had reached sufficient sequencing depth were used for final analysis.

For RNA-seq analysis, unmodified and unfiltered reads were aligned using STAR [45] (v2.7.9) to the GRCh38 reference genome and Ensembl version 107 annotation. Gene abundance estimates were calculated internal to the STAR aligner using the algorithm of HTSeq-count [46]. Gene expression was normalized and differential expression was tested using DESeq2 [47] utilizing the Wald test to contrast the groups. Differentially expressed genes were identified based on a threshold of the false discovery rate (FDR)<0.05, which corresponds to −Log10(P-value)≥2.745. Functional annotation and pathway enrichment analyses (including GO analysis and KEGG pathway analysis) were performed using the DAVID bioinformatic tool [43].

### Statistical analyses

Statistical analyses were done using GraphPad Prism for bar graphs and P-value<0.05 was considered significant. For group comparison of gene expression in both proteomics and RNA-seq analyses, Benjamin-Hochberg correction was used to control the false-discovery rate. Additional details of statistical analyses for proteomics and RNA-seq were described in previous sections 2.8 and 2.9, respectively.

## RESULTS

### Experimental design and flight hardware for the SpaceX Crew-8 experiment

We investigated the effect of space microgravity on cardiac spheroids derived from hiPSCs by comparing the cell cultures with and without spaceflight exposure. Figure 1A provides a timeline and an overview of the SpaceX Crew-8 experiment design. We generated cryopreserved cardiac spheroids from hiPSCs, performed pre-flight post-thawing testing of the cell preparations, and thawed the cells on the ground before spaceflight. Cardiac spheroids were sent to the ISS through the SpaceX Crew-8 mission launched on March 3, 2024 and exposed to space microgravity for 8 days. Characterization of the cells was performed after the return of live cells.

The dual chamber 1-well BioCells (Figure 1B, BioServe Space Technologies) were used as the flight hardware. The BioCell has a cell chamber and a medium chamber with a filter membrane between the two chambers to separate the cells but allows medium exchange between the chambers. The BioCells were placed in Habitats (PHABs, BioServe Space Technologies) (3 BioCells/Habitat, Figure 1B) during incubation and transportation. The spaceflight cells were cultured in BioCells and live cells were returned to Earth after spaceflight exposure for 8 days. The parallel cultures in the same culture device were maintained on Earth and used as the ground control.

### The cryopreservation of 3D cardiomyocytes streamlined the space experiment process of cell preparation and characterization

To facilitate the space experiment, we implemented procedures for cryopreservation of 3D hiPSC-CMs and characterization of cell quality before and after cryopreservation (Figure 2A). In ground-based study, we evaluated cryopreservation of 3D hiPSC-CMs and cell culture using BioCells (Supplemental Results; Figures S1–3). After thawing, cardiac spheroids typically recovered beating after 2–4 days in suspension. The morphology of these cultures was similar to that of parallel non-cryopreserved cultures with some of spheroids becoming irregular overtime in shape/arrangement (Figure S1). The changes in morphology did not affect cell viability as shown in Live/Dead staining (Figure S2). For the spaceflight experiment, hiPSCs were induced for cardiomyocyte differentiation and cardiac spheroids were generated in microwells on differentiation day 9 and cryopreserved on differentiation day 11 (Figure 2B).

To evaluate the quality of the cell preparations, we initially characterized the cells on differentiation day 6 (Level I QC) to examine the purity of cardiac progenitors by immunocytochemistry analysis of NKX2.5, a transcription factor associated with cardiac progenitors. We then performed post-thawing testing to examine the survival and purity of cardiomyocytes (Level II QC).

Efficient differentiation induction was achieved as detected by immunocytochemistry analysis on differentiation day 6; 89% of the cells were positive for NKX2.5, a cardiac progenitor marker (Figure 2C). For post-thawing testing, the spheroids recovered beating 4 days after thawing and contained high purity (83% a-actinin-positive cells) of cardiomyocytes as detected by immunocytochemistry analysis of α-actinin, a cardiac structural protein (Figure 2D).

### Pre-flight preparation, ISS operation, and sample return proceeded successfully

Cryopreserved cardiac spheroids were first thawed at home lab (Emory University) and then transported to the launch site, the Space Station Processing Facility (SSPF) at Kennedy Space Center (KSC). ISS cultures of cardiac spheroids were loaded into BioCells (n=3). Parallel cultures of cardiac spheroids in BioCells (n=3) were prepared as a backup set of spaceflight cultures due to possible launch slips/scrub. One set of these cells was ultimately used as the ground control. BioCells were positioned in Habitats (PHABs) and stored in an incubator (37°C and 5% CO2) before launch. As part of the pre-flight quality control, beating cells were observed from the BioCell cultures before handover to NASA. During transportation of the cells, the Habitats were sealed to maintain CO2 levels.

The medium syringes were loaded at the launch site and frozen at −80°C following kit integration of materials/supplies for flight operations. During launch and on the ISS, the medium syringes were stored at −95°C until flight operations. A spare kit of medium syringes was launched in the event of an undock delay but was not needed and discarded once the payload was returned.

The BioServe launch site team performed the final quality control review at the SSPF. Other procedures proceeded normally, including L-72h (72 h before launch) handover of medium syringe kits to the NASA team, L-36h initial handover of BioCells, and the second handover for the replacement of the initial ISS set with the backup ISS set, and launch (March 3, 2024).

Once on the ISS, the cells were maintained in the SABL1 incubator (37°C/5% CO2). Medium exchange (30 mL/BioCell) on the ISS was successfully performed 4 days post launch. During the medium exchange operation, medium was thawed and then warmed to ambient temperature. BioCells (in Habitats) were placed at ambient temperature before medium exchange. BioCells were imaged the following day (5 days post launch), and beating spheroids were observed and captured by video on the ISS (Supplemental Movie 1).

During sample return from the ISS, the spaceflight cultures in BioCells were maintained at 37°C in sealed Habitats. The cells went through 8 days of space microgravity starting from launch day. At KSC, medium exchange was performed before the transportation of spaceflight cultures to Emory University. For the ground control, material preparation and operation were performed similarly to mimic the fight operation procedures. Upon cell return, both the spaceflight and ground control cultures had beating spheroids. The cell and medium samples were harvested for RNA-Seq and proteomics analyses, and the remaining cells were used for live cell imaging.

### Spaceflight did not affect cardiac cell contraction and Ca2+ transients of cardiac spheroids

Ca2+ transients are key functional characteristics of cardiomyocytes [48] and the driving force behind cardiac cell contraction. To examine if spaceflight affected the function of hiPSC-CMs, we performed 3D live cell imaging using a home-built Fourier light-field microscopy (FLFM) system [33]. FLFM takes elemental images from multiple perspectives of the sample, projecting all 3D information onto a 2D frame, from which the entire sample volume can be computationally retrieved. Taking advantage of this scanning-free 3D imaging scheme, we were enabled to perform high-speed (125 Hz, see 2.8) volumetric recording of the 3D hiPSC-CMs in both groups with subcellular resolution (Figures 3A and 3B, and Supplemental Movie 2), extracting the Ca2+ transient and moving trajectory of each individual cell (Figures 3A vi–viii and 3B vi–viii) in the spheroids. From the profiles of the Ca2+ signals and motion trajectories of cells from both groups, we acquired the characteristics of their Ca2+ traits and contractility, including peak amplitude, time to peak, peak to half decay time, maximum rise slope, and maximum decay slope (Figures 3C and S4). By statistically analyzing and comparing these indicators of cells from the ground culture and those from the spaceflight culture, we concluded that cells in the spaceflight culture had normal contraction index and Ca2+ transients.

### Spaceflight upregulated proteins involved in cell survival, proliferation, and metabolic pathways

To examine the molecular changes induced by spaceflight, we conducted proteomic analysis to compare protein abundance in the spaceflight and ground samples. Pearson correlation analysis indicated high reproducibility among the biological triplicates of cell lysate samples in each group (Pearson correlation coefficient=0.97 to 1; Figure 4A). Compared with the ground control, the spaceflight cell cultures had 698 upregulated proteins and 714 downregulated proteins (Figure 4B).

Among the top upregulated proteins based on fold changes (Table S1), several were involved in metabolism, cell survival against oxidative stress, autophagy, and apoptosis, including UGT2A3 (UDP glucuronosyltransferase family 2 member A3), ADH1A (alcohol dehydrogenase 1A) [49], CEBPD (CCAAT/enhancer-binding protein delta) [50], and EEF2K (eukaryotic elongation factor 2 kinase/Ca2+/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase, CAMKIII) [51, 52]. Specifically, UGT2A3 is an enzyme with glucuronosyltransferase activity that allows lipophilic substrates to conjugate with glucuronic acid, increasing their water solubility and enhancing elimination of potentially toxic compounds from cells. In addition, the activity of EEF2K depends on calcium ions and calmodulin and is cytoprotective for cancer cells against nutrient starvation and other stress conditions by inhibiting apoptosis and promoting cancer cell survival [53].

Additionally, several proteins related to proliferation were identified in the top upregulated proteins, such as KRT13 (Keratin 13) [54] and PRIM1 (DNA primase subunit 1) [55] (Figure 4B and Table S1). KRT13 is an intermediate filament protein that supports structural integrity and stemness of cancer cells, inducing breast cancer metastasis through increased breast cancer cell proliferation [54]. PRIM1 as a key regulator of cell proliferation is involved in the initiation step of the DNA replication process through activation of the G2/M cell cycle checkpoint. It promotes tumorigenesis and progression through the growth of cancer cells, such as hepatocellular carcinoma cells [55] and breast cancer [56]. Consistently, proteins with negative effect on cell proliferation and survival were downregulated, including PCDH18 (protocadherin 18, Table S2). In colorectal cancer cells, overexpression of PCDH18 inhibited cell viability, colony formation and migration, while knockdown of PCDH18 enhanced the clonogenicity and migration [57].

We also performed Gene ontology (GO) analysis and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) analysis using DAVID bioinformatics resources [43]. Among regulated proteins, the following biological processes are highly enriched: sarcomere organization, regulation of cell proliferation, cardiac muscle contraction, regulation of stem cell proliferation, protein folding, actin cytoskeleton organization, stress-activated MAPK cascade, ventricular cardiac muscle tissue morphogenesis, and response to oxidative stress, while RNA splicing was found in both upregulated and downregulated proteins (Figure 4C). There were 10 upregulated proteins associated with biological process of regulation of cell proliferation, including SHH (sonic hedgehog signaling molecule), TGFB1 (transforming growth factor beta 1) and TPD52L2 (tumor protein D52 like 2) (Table S3). Among upregulated proteins, based on cellular component, the following GO terms are overrepresented: cytoskeleton, mitochondrion, focal adhesion, and sarcomere (Figure 4D). There were 62 upregulated proteins associated with the GO term of mitochondrion, including MIEF1 (mitochondrial elongation factor 1), SNAP23 (synaptosome associated protein 23) and HIP1R (huntingtin interacting protein 1 related) (Table S4). The enriched GO terms of molecular function included lipid binding, ubiquitin binding, and actin binding while protein binding and RNA binding were found in both upregulated and downregulated proteins (Figure 4E). KEGG pathway analysis demonstrated that pathways were largely enriched in those involved in metabolic pathways, amino acid synthesis, actin cytoskeleton, fluid shear stress, and autophagy (Figure 4F). There were 90 proteins associated with enriched metabolic pathways, including PTGDS (prostaglandin D2 synthase), SMYD2 (SET and MYND domain containing 2) and RDH10 (Retinol dehydrogenase 10) (Table S5). Downregulated proteins were associated with KEGG pathways of N-glycan biosynthesis and ECM-receptor interaction (Figure 4F).

Similar results were observed using another independent bioinformatics tool for pathway and process enrichment analysis by MetaScape [44]. Upregulated proteins in the cell lysate samples were enriched in proteasomes, pyruvate metabolism, arginine biosynthesis, cysteine and methionine metabolism, glutathione metabolism, drug metabolism, biosynthesis of amino acids, autophagy, and DNA replication (Figure S5A). Downregulated proteins in the cell lysate samples were enriched in various types of N-glycan biosynthesis and ECM-receptor interaction (Figure S5B).

We also performed secretome analysis by proteomics using cell culture medium samples collected in spaceflight cultures and the ground control. Pearson correlation analysis indicated consistency and reproducibility among biological triplicates of the samples in each group (Pearson correlation coefficient=0.97 to 1; Figure 4G). Compared with the ground control, the spaceflight samples had 14 upregulated proteins and 20 downregulated proteins (Figure 4H and Table S6). Among them, HSPA1L (heat shock protein family A [Hsp70] member 1 like) was detected in the top upregulated proteins. HSPA1L plays a role in promoting cancer cell proliferation and apoptosis-resistance [58]. In addition, several upregulated proteins, including PSAT1 (phosphoserine aminotransferase 1), GAPDH (glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase), and ALDOC1 (aldolase, fructose-bisphosphate C), are involved in biosynthesis of amino acids (Table S6).

Taking together, the proteomic analysis indicates that proteins involved in cell survival, proliferation, and metabolism were significantly upregulated in 3D hiPSC-CMs following the spaceflight exposure.

### Spaceflight upregulated genes involved in cardiac development and structure, mitochondrion, and metabolism associated with cell survival

To further investigate the effect of spaceflight on hiPSC-CM spheroids, we performed RNA-Seq analyses using RNA isolated from spaceflight cultures and the ground control (n=3 biological replicates per group). To identify differentially expressed genes (DEGs), the false discovery rate (FDR)<0.05 was used as the threshold which corresponded to −Log10(P-value)≥2.745. With this method, we identified 526 DEGs (160 upregulated and 366 downregulated) in the spaceflight samples compared with the ground control (Figures 5A and S6).

Among the top upregulated DEGs, several genes were associated with cardiac development and structure (Figure 5A and Table S7). For example, spaceflight upregulated TNNT2 (cardiac troponin T) (Figure 5A), the tropomyosin-binding subunit of the troponin complex that regulates muscle contraction in response to alterations in intracellular calcium ion concentrations. Spaceflight also upregulated CPNE5 (Copine 5) (Figure 5A), a member of the copine calcium-dependent, phospholipid-binding family of proteins that act as membrane trafficking binding proteins [59]. Other top upregulated genes included PLCB2 (phospholipase C beta 2) which is an essential component of the plasma membrane of all mammalian cells, including the cardiac sarcolemma, contributing to cytoskeleton organization, cell growth, and ion channel regulation.

Several top upregulated DEGs were correlated with cellular proliferation and survival, including CDH17 (cadherin 17), SFRP5 (secreted frizzled related protein 5), CEACAM5 (CEA cell adhesion molecule 5), and NRIP2 (nuclear receptor interacting protein 2) (Figure 5A and Table S7). In colon cancer cells, CDH17 regulates integrin signaling to stimulate cell proliferation [60]. It also plays a critical role in the proliferation of vascular cells in vitro and in vivo [61]. Overexpression of SFRP5 in a mouse model inhibits ischemic injury, reduces risk of cardiac rupture, and improves cardiac function through inhibiting mitochondrial dysfunction [62]. CEACAM5 is highly expressed in many cancer cell types, and antibodies targeting CEACAM5 inhibit cancer cell adhesion, invasion, and metastasis [63]. In colorectal cancer, NRIP2 interacts with molecules in the Wnt pathway and mediates the self-renewal of cancer cells via the Wnt activation [64].

In addition, the top upregulated DEGs included genes associated with metabolism, such as PLA2G4F (phospholipase A2 group IVF), GPAT2 (glycerol-3-phosphate acyltransferase 2, mitochondrial), PLCB2 [phospholipase C beta 2, which plays a role in the metabolism of inositol lipids [65], and ADAM11 (ADAM metallopeptidase domain 11) (Figure 5A and Table S7).

Among downregulated genes, several were involved in apoptosis and negative regulation of cell proliferation, including NNMT (nicotinamide N-methyltransferase), LIN01614 and PTX3 (pentraxin 3) (Figure 5A and Table S8). In liver cancer cells, NNMT knockdown improved cell survival by augmenting autophagy under nutrient starvation [66]. LINC01614 is a long noncoding RNA (lncRNA), inhibition of which promoted cell proliferation and repressed the apoptotic property in H9C2 cells upon hypoxia/reoxygenation treatment [67]. In an atherosclerotic cell model, suppression of PTX3 reduced inflammation and apoptosis mediated by the IkB kinase (IKK)/IkB/nuclear factor-kB (NF-kB) pathway [68]. Therefore, downregulation of these genes possibly played a role in protecting cells against space-mediated stress condition.

We further analyzed the DEGs by GO term analysis and KEGG analysis. In the category of biological process, several GO terms related to cardiomyocyte differentiation and development were enriched, including GO terms of sarcomere organization, cell-cell adhesion and heart development (Figure 5B). GO terms associated with cell survival and stress response were also enriched, such as cellular response to reactive oxygen species (Figure 5B). In the category of cellular component, the GO term of mitochondrion was enriched and associated with 16 DGEs (10% of total upregulated DEGs) (Figure 5C). GO terms of cellular components associated with cardiomyocytes were enriched, including M band, sarcomere, and cardiac myofibril (Figure 5C). GO terms associated with extracellular matrix were also enriched including collagen-containing extracellular matrix, collagen trimer, and collagen type IX trimer (Figure 5C). In the category of molecular function, metal ion binding was among the top enriched GO terms and was associated with 28 upregulated DEGs (18.9% of the total upregulated DEGs, Figure 5D). In addition, GO terms associated with cardiomyocyte function were enriched including voltage-gated calcium channel activity involved in regulation of presynaptic cytosolic calcium levels, high voltage-gated calcium channel activity, actin binding and titin binding (Figure 5D). Finally, KEGG pathway analysis revealed that spaceflight enriched pathways of cytoskeleton in muscle cells, phospholipase D signaling pathway, protein digestion and absorption, and pathways important for cell survival such as glycerophospholipid metabolism, and glycerolipid metabolism (Figure 5E).

These transcriptomic profiles indicate that spaceflight increased the expression of genes associated with cardiomyocyte development, cellular components of cardiac structure, mitochondrion, and metabolic pathways related to cell survival.

## Discussion

Since microgravity can significantly affect cell characteristics, there is a growing interest in leveraging it as a potential approach to improve various stem cell properties, including pluripotency, differentiation, and maturation of stem cell derivatives [69–72]. We hypothesized that space microgravity could alter molecular features of hiPSC-CMs and understanding these changes could facilitate their applications in regenerative medicine. To examine the effect of spaceflight on hiPSC-CMs, we sent hiPSC-derived cardiac spheroids to the ISS through the SpaceX Crew 8 mission. Astronauts successfully performed several procedures including medium exchange, microscopy, and live-cell return. Beating cardiac spheroids were observed on the ISS and upon their return to Earth. These beating cells had normal functional characteristics as analyzed by 3D live cell imaging of displacement (an index of cell contraction) and Ca2+ transients. By comparing the spaceflight samples with ground controls using proteomics and RNAseq analyses, we found that spaceflight significantly upregulated proteins and genes involved in cell survival and metabolic pathways.

In this study, upregulated proteins/genes and enriched pathways in spaceflight samples included those involved in stress response and metabolism which were previously recognized for cancer growth and progression. Since the comparison was done between spaceflight samples and ground control samples, other space environmental factors might have also contributed to the changes in spaceflight samples. The effect of microgravity on cell survival and proliferation has also been observed in previous studies. After a 30-day culture on the ISS, human cardiovascular progenitors exhibited improved cell proliferation which was associated with activation of the ERK and Akt pathways [27]. Compared with cells cultured under simulated ground condition on the ISS (ISS 1G control), hiPSC-derived cardiac progenitors cultured under ISS microgravity conditions for 3 weeks had improved cell proliferation and cardiac differentiation [29, 30]. Similarly, hiPSC-derived cardiac progenitors cultured under simulated microgravity using a random position machine also had increased proliferation compared with cells under standard gravity [73]. The cardiac progenitors under simulated microgravity also had increased expression of genes associated with cell survival such as heat shock proteins [73].

Improved cell survival and proliferation are inter-connected with changes in mitochondria and metabolic pathways. Mitochondria are powerhouses for almost all eukaryotic cells including cardiomyocytes, orchestrating cellular energy production and metabolism and controlling central processes of cell survival, cell cycle, and cell death [74]. Our observations of the positive effect of spaceflight on mitochondrion cellular component and metabolic pathways are consistent with previous studies. For example, a short-term exposure of 3D hiPSC-CMs to simulated microgravity for 1 week significantly increased mitochondrial function, mitochondrial content, and mitochondrial membrane potential [75]. A long-term culture (> 30 days) of late-stage 2D hiPSC-CMs on the ISS also increased gene expression associated with metabolism [31].

The current study provided details on molecular changes on the effect of spaceflight on mitochondria and metabolic pathways. Among upregulated proteins in 3D hiPSC-CMs following spaceflight, many are associated with cellular component GO term of mitochondrion (62 DEPs) and KEGG metabolic pathways (90 DEPs). Similarly, transcriptomics analysis also indicated enrichment of GO term of mitochondrion and pathways of glycerophospholipid metabolism and glycerolipid metabolism. Glycerophospholipid metabolism was critically important for cell survival and involved in hypoxic adaptation based on multi-omics analyses in multiple species including yeast, zebrafish and mice [76]. Other specific metabolic pathways enriched by spaceflight from the proteomic profiles included glutathione metabolism, biosynthesis of amino acids, and pyruvate metabolism, which are involved in cell survival. For example, glutathione metabolism is highly critical for antioxidant defense and cell survival [77]. Biosynthesis of amino acids is essential for proliferation and survival of mammalian cells [78]. Pyruvate is a key molecule responsible for ATP production in mitochondria [79]. In addition, spaceflight enriched AMPK signaling pathway, a master regulator of metabolism [80]. Activation of AMPK in hiPSC-CMs increased metabolic maturation and enabled to model cardiac disease associated with metabolic remodeling [81].

For cardiac regeneration using cell therapy, finding strategies to improve cell survival is highly significant. Since many stress factors can cause cell death right after the cell transplantation [82–84], substantial efforts have been devoted to develop strategies to improve graft survival of cardiomyocytes upon transplantation [23]. The results from our comprehensive proteomics and transcriptomics analyses indicate that spaceflight significantly upregulated proteins involved in regulation of cell stress response and survival signaling in 3D hiPSC-CMs. These changes were associated with significant upregulation of metabolic pathways and cellular component of mitochondrion. This study also highlights the need for future research using other analytical methods to examine metabolomic profiles, cell proliferation/survival, changes in expression of molecular pathways together with upstream and downstream signals, and mitochondrial function of human cardiac spheroids. These future studies would facilitate understanding the role of metabolic remodeling in cell survival and growth characteristics of hiPSC-CMs under stress conditions. In addition, comparison between cardiomyocytes and non-cardiac cells in response to space environment could identify cell type-specific molecular changes under space environment. Such studies may help develop new approaches to produce hiPSC-CMs on Earth with improved cell survival ability by controlling their cellular response to stress conditions and reducing cell damages via metabolomics mechanism. In addition, the evaluation of survival of spaceflight cells under pathological stress could provide proof-of-concept to demonstrate the beneficial impact of space microgravity. The findings from this study provide strong support for these future efforts on space experiments.

In addition, the approaches developed in this study, such as cryopreservation of cardiac spheroids, will pave the way to facilitate future space experiments. Cryopreservation has several advantages since it allows to generate sufficient cells before launch and ensures that cells with good quality are used for space experiments [85]. This procedure also increases flexibility in scheduling for space experiments since cryopreserved cells can be thawed when needed. In this study, 3D hiPSC-CMs were generated using microscale tissue engineering and cryopreserved in a serum-free solution. During cell preparation and testing, we characterized the cells in multiple steps. We initially characterized cells before cryopreservation (Level I QC on day 6 post differentiation) by examining the purity of cardiac progenitors (efficiency of cardiac differentiation). Cell batches with high purities of cardiac progenitors were cryopreserved and then tested post-thawing (Level II QC) to monitor cell morphology and cardiomyocyte purity. During preflight testing, the cryopreserved cardiac spheroids survived well and differentiated efficiently into cardiomyocytes following thawing. We expect that the cryopreservation strategy can be helpful for experimental designs of other cell types in space experiments, particularly for 3D cells such as organoids. More broadly, cryopreservation of 3D cells is also highly desirable for regenerative medicine, since it allows sufficient pre-characterization to ensure that only cell preparations with high quality are selected for transplantation to meet the high standard of clinical requirements.

In conclusion, the findings in this study provide important insights about the role of the space environment on the regulation of proteins/genes associated with improved cell survival and metabolism. The molecular changes included enrichment of molecules/pathways involved in cellular stress/survival responses, regulation of cell proliferation, cardiac structure, mitochondrion, and metabolic pathways. Further understanding of these molecular changes may lead to new discoveries to produce better cells on Earth for cardiac regeneration.
